usageSteps.title: Upload a photo
usageSteps.body:
Drag a photo into the upload area at the top of the page, or click to choose one. JPG, PNG, and most camera RAW formats are supported,
with up to 100MB per file. Your photo is never sent to a server — everything is processed inside your browser.

usageSteps.title: Read the EXIF data
usageSteps.body:
As soon as the photo loads, the camera, lens, shutter speed, aperture, ISO, focal length, and the date and time taken appear in the “Extracted EXIF” panel.
Photos that went through a messaging app or social network may have had their metadata removed, so some fields might not appear.

usageSteps.title: See where it was taken on a map
usageSteps.body:
If the photo contains GPS data, click “View on map” next to the location row to see exactly where it was shot.
Photos without location data leave this row empty.

usageSteps.title: Calculate your ND filter exposure
usageSteps.body:
The ND filter calculator shows the shutter speed detected from your photo as the base value. Pick a filter strength or type in a custom number of stops to get the long-exposure
shutter speed you need in the field, then use the built-in timer while you shoot. Matching gear recommendations for the selected ND filter are shown too.

usageSteps.title: Build a camera-info frame
usageSteps.body:
Use “Create a frame” in the top menu, or the button that appears after uploading, to open the EXIF Frame Generator. Add a clean camera-info frame to your photo
and download it at the original resolution — handy for social media and portfolios.

usageSteps.title: Protect your privacy before sharing
usageSteps.body:
EXIF data can include where and when a photo was taken and what device shot it, so sharing the original file can expose personal information.
Remove the metadata with the EXIF / Metadata Remover before you post.

usageSteps.title: Explore more tools and guides
usageSteps.body:
Depth-of-field, golden hour, crop factor, and exposure stops calculators, plus an image compressor, are all free in the Tools menu.
Read the guides for exposure, ND filters, and genre-by-genre shooting tips, and check the FAQ for quick answers.

faq.question: Do I need to create an account to use ExifLens?
faq.answer: No. ExifLens works entirely without sign-up — just open the page and drop in a photo.

faq.question: Are my photos uploaded to a server?
faq.answer: No. Every calculation and every pixel of processing happens locally in your browser. Your photos never leave your device.

faq.question: What image formats does ExifLens support?
faq.answer: JPG and PNG are fully supported, along with most common camera RAW formats (ARW, CR2, CR3, NEF, RAF, RW2, ORF, DNG, PEF, SRW).

faq.question: How does the ND filter calculator work?
faq.answer: Enter your base (unfiltered) shutter speed and pick the ND filter strength you're using — the calculator instantly shows the new shutter speed needed for the same exposure, plus an optional countdown timer for the shot.

faq.question: Can I customize the frame before downloading?
faq.answer: Yes. Every theme's colors, font, padding, and brand logo visibility can be adjusted, and you can edit any of the text fields shown on the frame without changing the EXIF data itself.

faq.question: Is ExifLens free to use?
faq.answer: Yes, completely free. The site is supported by ads and occasional affiliate links, which never affect how the tools themselves work.

sections.heading: What is ExifLens
body: ExifLens is a free, browser-based toolkit for photographers. It reads the EXIF metadata embedded in your photos, helps you calculate long-exposure times for neutral density (ND) filters, and lets you generate clean, shareable frames that display your camera settings alongside the photo.

sections.heading: Why We Built It
body: We wanted a fast, no-signup tool that respects your photos — everything runs locally in your browser, so your images are never uploaded anywhere. No accounts, no watermarks you didn't ask for, no waiting on a server.

sections.heading: The Photographer Behind ExifLens
body: ExifLens is built and run by a working photographer who shoots landscapes, cityscapes and autumn color under the name Chronicle of Moments_SH. Every tool on this site began as a small problem in the field: working out an ND filter exposure at the water's edge, checking how wide a lens really is on a crop body, or finding out exactly when the sun would line up with a subject.

The photographs below are our own work, and the watermark in each corner is the same name behind our guides. They are here so you can judge who is writing the advice you read: not stock illustrations, but frames that taught us the lessons we write about.

story.heading: How I Got Into Photography
story.intro: I did not start out as a photographer. This is how a camera bought for shop product photos turned into travel, landscape and video work, told in the order the gear changed.

steps.body: I bought my first camera, a Canon EOS 800D, together with a Canon EF 40mm f/2.8 STM prime lens, for my online shop. I only shot product photos, so the camera saw little use, and when the business closed it drifted out of my hands.
On my first trip abroad, a visit to Tokyo with a friend, I caught the photography bug and pulled the old 800D back out.

I took the camera on my own to Tokyo. My life with a camera started after that trip. Back home I kept practicing with a Sigma 18-35mm F1.8 DC HSM | Art (bought new) and a Sigma 30mm F1.4 DC HSM | Art (bought used).

Gear fever set in. I sold the 800D with its EF-S 18-55mm kit lens, the EF 40mm f/2.8 STM and some accessories, and bought a Canon EOS R7 with the RF-S18-150mm F3.5-6.3 IS STM kit lens. A Canon Control Ring Mount Adapter EF-EOS R let me keep using the Sigma lenses.

In May I added a camera dehumidifier cabinet and a heipi tripod to get ready to shoot more seriously, and in June I bought the RF24-70mm F2.8 L IS USM and a HOYA 82mm UV, CPL and ND filter kit. In July I bought a DJI Osmo Action 4 Adventure Combo and took it on my August trip to Thailand. September brought the RF15-35mm F2.8 L IS USM and, after a second six-night Thailand trip, the RF70-200mm F2.8 L IS USM at the end of the month, which completed my wide, standard and telephoto zooms. I also kept practicing with a DJI Mini 3 Pro drone.

I bought a DJI Air 3S and a DJI Osmo Pocket 3, and gave my Mini 3 Pro to a friend. My first month-long stay in Thailand was spent renting a motorbike and photographing all sorts of places. Many people asked to see my camera and video gear, and many asked me to take their photo.
A second month in Thailand. The country is much bigger than Korea, so there was always somewhere new to explore.
I added the Canon EOS R5 Mark II body, plus the RF100mm F2.8 L MACRO IS USM, RF35mm F1.4 L VCM and RF50mm F1.4 L VCM.
A third month-long stay in Thailand.

DofCalculator.aboutBody: Depth of field is the zone in front of and behind your focus point that still looks acceptably sharp. It depends on your focal length, aperture, subject distance, and sensor size (via the circle of confusion). This calculator uses the standard hyperfocal-distance formulas that most photography references and DoF calculator apps use. Results are estimates for typical viewing conditions — actual sharpness also depends on print size, viewing distance, and lens quality.
DofCalculator.disclaimer: For reference only. Real-world sharpness can vary with your specific lens and how the final image is viewed or printed.

faq.question: What is hyperfocal distance?
faq.answer: It's the focus distance that gives you the maximum depth of field for a given focal length and aperture — everything from half that distance to infinity appears acceptably sharp.

faq.question: Why does sensor size affect the result?
faq.answer: Smaller sensors need a smaller circle of confusion to look equally sharp when viewed at the same size, which changes the depth of field for the same focal length and aperture.

faq.question: Is this exact for my camera?
faq.answer: It's a close, industry-standard approximation. For critical work, treat the results as a starting point rather than an exact guarantee.

sections.heading: How the calculation works
body: The calculator first finds the hyperfocal distance, H = f²/(N·c) + f, where f is focal length, N is the f-number and c is the circle of confusion set by sensor size. For a subject distance s it then finds the near limit Dn = H·s/(H+(s−f)) and the far limit Df = H·s/(H−(s−f)); the difference is the total depth of field.
When the subject distance reaches the hyperfocal distance or more, the far limit is shown as infinity. Enter the distance from the camera sensor (focal plane) to the subject.

sections.heading: Worked examples
list: On full frame (circle of confusion 0.03 mm), a 50 mm lens at f/1.8 focused at 2 m has a hyperfocal distance of about 46.3 m. The sharp zone runs from about 1.92 m to 2.09 m, a total depth of field of only about 17 cm.
An 85 mm lens at f/1.8 on a portrait subject 3 m away gives roughly 2.94 m to 3.07 m (about 13 cm). That is why you need to place focus precisely on the eyes.
A 24 mm lens at f/11 focused at 3 m has a hyperfocal distance of about 1.77 m, so the far limit is infinity and the near limit is about 1.12 m. Everything from 1.12 m to infinity is sharp.

With the same 50 mm, f/8 and 2 m, full frame gives about 1.69 m to 2.46 m (about 77 cm), while Micro Four Thirds (circle of confusion 0.015 mm) gives about 1.83 m to 2.21 m (about 38 cm). Sensor size changes the result.

sections.heading: When to use it
body: For landscapes, use it to find where to focus so a nearby flower and a distant mountain are both sharp. For portraits, use it to judge how far to open the aperture for enough background blur. Before buying a lens you can also compare the depth of field of f/1.4 and f/2.8 at the same angle of view in numbers.

sections.heading: Limits and common mistakes
list: The circle of confusion is a viewing-condition reference value. If you print large or zoom in far, the truly sharp zone can be narrower than calculated.
Stopping down too far softens the whole image through diffraction. Closing to f/22 for more depth of field is not always a gain.
The calculation assumes focus lands exactly where you aimed. With shallow depth of field, small autofocus errors change the result a lot.
Choosing a sensor size that does not match your camera shifts the result. On a crop body, check the sensor size first.
Enter the real focal length printed on the lens, not an equivalent value.

ExposureCalculator.invalidInput: Enter valid, positive numbers for every field.
ExposureCalculator.pageDescription: See the equivalent shutter speed, aperture, or ISO you need when you change one exposure setting, so your shot stays exactly as bright.
ExposureCalculator.aboutBody: Aperture, shutter speed, and ISO form the ‘exposure triangle’ — each one can be adjusted by a stop to let in twice (or half) as much light. This calculator starts from a baseline exposure you know is correctly exposed, lets you pick one setting to change for a creative reason (like a faster shutter speed to freeze motion, or a wider aperture for background blur), and calculates exactly how much to adjust a second setting so the final image stays just as bright — while the third setting stays untouched.
ExposureCalculator.disclaimer: Assumes ideal reciprocity between settings. Extremely long exposures can show reciprocity failure on some cameras/film, and this calculator does not account for that.

faq.question: What does ‘a stop’ mean?
faq.answer: One stop is a doubling or halving of the light reaching your sensor — one full click on most aperture, shutter speed, or ISO dials.

faq.question: Why does the aperture calculation use a factor of 2?
faq.answer: Light passes through a lens opening, so it scales with area, not diameter — that’s why the f-number needs to change more than shutter speed or ISO to represent the same one-stop change.

faq.question: Can I freeze motion without changing my exposure?
faq.answer: Yes — set ‘Change’ to Shutter Speed and pick a faster speed, then choose Aperture or ISO to compensate with, and the calculator gives you the exact value that keeps the same brightness.

ExposureCalculator.exampleLeftAlt: Freeze-motion photo made with a fast shutter speed
ExposureCalculator.exampleRightAlt: Motion-blur photo made with a slow shutter speed

sections.heading: How the calculation works
body: Exposure is the sum of the brightness that aperture, shutter speed and ISO produce. The calculator converts all three to the same unit, the stop. Doubling shutter time or ISO adds one stop, while aperture follows the area of the opening, so it scales with the inverse square of the f-number. That is why going from f/4 to f/2.8 adds one stop.

You pick one setting you want to change and one setting to compensate with. The third stays at its baseline value, and the calculator finds the compensating value that keeps overall brightness the same.

sections.heading: Worked examples
list: From a baseline of f/4, 1/125 s and ISO 400, raising shutter speed to 1/500 s to freeze motion (2 stops) needs f/2 to compensate with aperture while ISO stays fixed.
From the same baseline, opening to f/2 (2 stops) and compensating with shutter speed gives 1/500 s. It agrees with the example above.
From the same baseline, lowering ISO to 100 (2 stops) while keeping aperture fixed means slowing the shutter to about 1/31 s (roughly 1/30 s) for the same brightness.
From f/8, 1/60 s and ISO 200, opening to f/2.8 adds about 3 stops, so compensating with shutter speed while ISO stays fixed gives about 1/490 s (roughly 1/500 s).

sections.heading: When to use it
body: It is most useful when you already know a correct exposure and want to change a setting for a creative reason, such as more background blur or frozen motion, without changing brightness. It is also a good way to build intuition for how the three settings relate while you practice manual mode.

sections.heading: Limits and common mistakes
list: It assumes your baseline exposure is already right. If the baseline is off, the result is off by the same amount.
Many cameras use 1/3-stop steps, so choose the available setting closest to the calculated value. A small difference is usually not a problem.
In very long exposures, reciprocity failure can make the image darker than calculated, and this calculator does not account for it.
Changing aperture also changes depth of field, raising ISO adds noise and changing shutter speed changes how motion looks. The same brightness does not mean the same photo.
You cannot pick the same setting for both the one you change and the one that compensates.

TimelapseCalculator.invalidInput: Enter valid, positive numbers for the fields above.
TimelapseCalculator.advancedSubtitle: Optional — estimate storage needs and preview how smooth the motion will look.
TimelapseCalculator.qualityChoppy: Low ratio — frames will look sharp but the played-back motion may appear choppy or strobe-like.
TimelapseCalculator.qualityCinematic: Around the classic 180° shutter angle — a natural, cinematic amount of motion blur.
TimelapseCalculator.qualitySmooth: High ratio — frames will show heavy motion blur, producing very smooth (sometimes dreamy) motion.
TimelapseCalculator.pageDescription: Work out your shooting interval, total frames, and shoot duration from your target video length, then estimate storage needs and motion blur — all in your browser.
TimelapseCalculator.aboutBody: A time-lapse shoot has three linked numbers: how often you trigger the shutter (interval), how long you shoot for, and how many frames you end up with — knowing any two gives you the third. This calculator also converts your frame count into a final video length at your chosen frame rate, estimates how much storage the shoot will need, and shows the ‘shutter angle’ — the ratio between your shutter speed and interval — which determines whether the played-back motion looks smooth and cinematic or sharp and strobe-like.
TimelapseCalculator.disclaimer: Estimates only. Actual file sizes vary by camera, format, and compression settings, and ‘ideal’ motion blur is a matter of creative taste.

faq.question: How do I pick a good interval?
faq.answer: It depends on how fast your subject moves — clouds and sunsets often work well around 3–10 seconds, while very slow scenes (construction, plant growth) may use minutes between shots. Start with the video duration you want and let this calculator work backward from there.

faq.question: Why does my video length come out shorter than I expected?
faq.answer: Video duration depends on both your total shots and your chosen frame rate — the same number of shots plays back faster (and shorter) at 60fps than at 24fps.

faq.question: What is a 180° shutter angle and why does it matter?
faq.answer: It’s the traditional film-industry standard where your shutter speed is exactly half your frame interval, producing motion blur that looks natural to viewers. This calculator’s shutter angle result tells you how close your settings are to that look.

TimelapseCalculator.exampleLeftAlt: Long-exposure night sky timelapse frame with star trails
TimelapseCalculator.exampleRightAlt: Fast-moving clouds captured across a timelapse sequence

sections.heading: How the calculation works
body: Shot count equals shooting time divided by interval. Knowing any two of the three fixes the third, and when you enter interval and duration the shot count is rounded down. Video length is shot count divided by frame rate (fps), and storage is shot count × file size per shot, divided by 1,024 to get GB.

Shutter angle is your shutter speed divided by the interval. A 100% ratio counts as 360°. Under 30% is flagged as choppy, 30 to 70% as a natural cinematic amount, and over 70% as smooth with heavy motion blur.

sections.heading: Worked examples
list: With the defaults, a 5 s interval over 60 minutes gives 720 shots, and at 24 fps the video runs 30 s. At 25 MB per shot, storage is about 17.58 GB.
A 3-hour sunset at an 8 s interval is 1,350 shots. At 30 fps that is 45 s of video, and about 32.96 GB at 25 MB per shot.
To make a 10 s video at 24 fps you need 240 frames. Shooting for 30 minutes (1,800 s), set the interval to 7.5 s.
With a 5 s interval and a 1/50 s shutter, the ratio is only 0.4%, which is choppy. With a 2 s interval and a 1 s shutter, the ratio is 50% (180°), a cinematic amount.

sections.heading: When to use it
body: It is most useful when you decide the video length first and work backward to the shots, interval and storage you need. It also helps when you want to try different intervals for scenes that change at different speeds, such as clouds and sunsets.

sections.heading: Limits and common mistakes
list: The interval has to be longer than the exposure time. If it is shorter than your shutter speed, the camera cannot keep up.
The camera also needs time to save each photo, so do not set the interval exactly equal to the shutter speed. Leave some margin.
A scene that goes from day to night changes brightness a lot, so shutter speed changes too. Keep in mind that shutter angle is based on a single shutter speed.
Storage is an estimate from the file size you enter. It can differ from reality depending on camera and format.
Also check that your battery and memory card are enough for the whole shooting time.

AstroCalculator.npfStricterNote: The NPF rule gives a shorter (more conservative) exposure time here — on high-resolution sensors, star trails become visible sooner than the simple 500 rule suggests.
AstroCalculator.npfLooserNote: The NPF rule gives a longer exposure time here — on lower-resolution sensors, pixels are large enough that a bit more exposure is still safe.
AstroCalculator.invalidInput: Enter valid, positive numbers for every field.
AstroCalculator.pageDescription: Get the longest shutter speed before stars start trailing, using both the simple 500 rule and the more accurate NPF rule — entirely in your browser.
AstroCalculator.aboutBody: Because the earth rotates, any exposure that’s too long will render stars as short trails instead of sharp points. The classic ‘500 rule’ (500 ÷ full-frame-equivalent focal length) is a quick, simple estimate. The ‘NPF rule’ is more accurate, especially on today’s high-resolution sensors, because it also factors in your aperture and your camera’s actual pixel pitch — smaller pixels reveal trailing sooner than the 500 rule accounts for.
AstroCalculator.disclaimer: Both rules are estimates for a ‘no visible trailing at normal viewing size’ standard — extreme pixel-peeping, very large prints, or unusually long lenses may need a shorter exposure than either rule suggests.

faq.question: Why do the 500 rule and NPF rule give different answers?
faq.answer: The 500 rule only considers focal length and crop factor. The NPF rule also accounts for your aperture and your camera’s pixel pitch, which is why two cameras with the same focal length but different resolutions get different NPF results.

faq.question: Which rule should I trust more?
faq.answer: The NPF rule is generally considered more accurate, especially on modern high-megapixel cameras, since smaller pixels make star trailing visible at shorter exposure times than the simple 500 rule assumes.

faq.question: I don’t know my camera’s exact megapixel count — what do I do?
faq.answer: Pick the resolution preset closest to your camera’s actual megapixel count; the listed example models can help you match it.

AstroCalculator.exampleLeftAlt: Milky Way photographed with pinpoint stars using a short exposure
AstroCalculator.exampleRightAlt: Night sky photo showing star trails from an overly long exposure

sections.heading: How the calculation works
body: The 500 rule gives exposure time in seconds as 500 ÷ (focal length × crop factor). The NPF rule uses (35 × f-number + 30 × pixel pitch in μm) ÷ focal length, so it accounts for your aperture and the real size of your sensor's pixels.

Pixel pitch is sensor width divided by horizontal pixel count, and the pixel count comes from megapixels and aspect ratio. The closer your sensor size and resolution presets are to your camera, the closer the result is to reality.

sections.heading: Worked examples
list: Full frame, 24 mm f/2.8, about 45 MP (pixel pitch about 4.4 μm): the 500 rule gives about 21 s and the NPF rule about 9.6 s. The higher the resolution, the bigger the gap.
The same lens on a roughly 24.2 MP full-frame body (about 6.0 μm) stretches the NPF result to about 12 s. Fewer megapixels mean larger pixels, so a slightly longer exposure is still safe.
Full frame, 14 mm f/2.8, about 61 MP (about 3.8 μm): 500 rule about 36 s, NPF about 15 s.
APS-C (crop 1.5), 16 mm f/2.8, about 33 MP (about 3.3 μm): 500 rule about 21 s, NPF about 12 s.

sections.heading: When to use it
body: Before heading out for the Milky Way or star photos, work out the maximum exposure for each lens and camera combination so you are not calculating in the dark on location. Seeing both rules side by side also shows which one is more conservative.

sections.heading: Limits and common mistakes
list: Both rules estimate whether stars look like points at normal viewing size. If you print large or view at 100%, shoot shorter.

The estimates assume a sky near the celestial equator. Stars near the celestial pole, such as around Polaris, move more slowly and can take longer exposures, while stars near the celestial equator trail faster.
On a crop body, enter the real focal length; the crop factor is applied through the sensor size you pick. Entering an equivalent focal length counts it twice.
A shorter exposure gathers less light. How to balance it with a wider aperture and higher ISO is a separate decision.
If you do not know your exact megapixel count, choose the closest preset. A small difference barely changes the result.

BracketCalculator.invalidInput: Enter valid, positive numbers for every field.
BracketCalculator.advancedSubtitle: See a dynamic-range guide and an estimated total shooting time.
BracketCalculator.dynamicRangeStandard: A standard range — most scenes can be captured well in a single exposure, so bracketing here is optional.
BracketCalculator.dynamicRangeHighContrast: A high-contrast scene — this is the range where HDR blending typically helps, such as a bright sky against a shaded foreground.
BracketCalculator.dynamicRangeExtreme: A very wide dynamic range — suited to extreme-contrast scenes like backlit silhouettes or a bright window against a dark interior. Consider adding more frames.
BracketCalculator.pageDescription: Enter a baseline exposure and a stop interval to automatically calculate the aperture, shutter speed, and ISO for every frame of an HDR exposure bracket.
BracketCalculator.aboutBody: HDR (High Dynamic Range) photography captures the same scene at several different exposures and blends them together, recovering both bright highlights and dark shadows that a single exposure can't hold at once. This calculator starts from a baseline exposure (aperture, shutter speed, ISO) and builds a bracket of frames by shifting one of those three parameters up and down by your chosen stop interval.
BracketCalculator.disclaimer: The number of frames and step sizes your camera's actual auto-exposure bracketing (AEB) feature supports varies by model. Treat these values as a reference and check your camera's real settings range before shooting.

faq.question: How many frames and what step size should I bracket with?
faq.answer: Three frames at ±1 stop is often enough for an ordinary scene. For high-contrast scenes like backlighting or sunsets, widen the step (±2 stops) or add more frames (7 or 9) to cover a wider brightness range.

faq.question: Should I bracket aperture, shutter speed, or ISO?
faq.answer: For static scenes on a tripod (like landscapes), shutter-speed bracketing is most common, since depth of field stays identical across frames. For handheld shots or scenes with movement, ISO bracketing can be worth considering instead.

faq.question: Why does this show an estimated total shooting time?
faq.answer: Long-exposure bracketing (for example, night landscapes) stretches each frame's exposure time, so a full bracket can take much longer than expected. This helps you plan around how long a tripod needs to stay in position, or how much a scene's light might shift during the sequence.

BracketCalculator.exampleLeftAlt: A camera mounted on a tripod outdoors, set up for exposure bracketing
BracketCalculator.exampleRightAlt: An HDR-blended photo combining several differently exposed frames

sections.heading: How the bracket list is built
body: The calculator puts your baseline exposure in the middle (0 EV) and adds frames above and below it, spaced by the step size you choose. Frame counts are limited to the odd numbers 3, 5, 7 and 9 so there is always a baseline frame, and step sizes are 1/3, 1/2, 1 or 2 stops.

Only one of aperture, shutter speed or ISO changes; the other two stay at their baseline values. Shutter speed and ISO double with every stop, while the f-number changes by about 1.41 times (√2) per stop but in the opposite direction. A brighter (+EV) frame uses a wider aperture, which means a smaller f-number.

sections.heading: Worked examples
list: Baseline 1/125 s, f/8, ISO 100 with shutter-speed bracketing, 5 frames at ±1 stop: the frames are about 1/500 s, 1/250 s, 1/125 s, 1/62 s and 1/31 s. The total brightness range is 4 stops, and with 1.5 s of overhead per shot the estimated total shooting time is about 7.6 s.
For a night scene with a 4 s baseline, the same 5-frame bracket gives 1 s, 2 s, 4 s, 8 s and 16 s. The exposures alone add up to 31 s, and with overhead the tripod has to stay still for about 38.5 s.
If you bracket aperture instead, starting from f/8, the +1 stop frame is about f/5.7 and the -1 stop frame is about f/11.

sections.heading: How to read the dynamic range guide
body: A total brightness range under 4 stops is labeled "standard": most scenes fit in a single exposure, so bracketing is optional. From 4 up to 8 stops it is "high contrast", the range where HDR blending helps with a bright sky over a shaded foreground. At 8 stops or more it is "very wide", for scenes like backlit silhouettes or a bright window in a dark room, where more frames are worth considering.
These categories are rules of thumb. How much a single frame can actually hold depends on your camera sensor and whether you shoot RAW.

sections.heading: Limits and common mistakes
list: For still scenes such as landscapes, shutter-speed bracketing is the safest choice. Changing aperture changes depth of field between frames, and changing ISO changes noise.
Even on a tripod, leaves in the wind or moving people can leave ghosting when you merge the frames. The more frames you shoot, the bigger the risk.
Your camera's automatic exposure bracketing (AEB) supports different frame counts and step sizes depending on the model. Treat the results as a reference and check the real settings range.
For long exposures, the longest frame may exceed your camera's maximum shutter speed. In that case consider bulb mode or a smaller step.
The default overhead of 1.5 s per shot is a typical estimate. If your camera clears its buffer slowly, raise the value yourself.

PrintResolutionCalculator.invalidInput: Enter valid, positive numbers for width, height, and DPI.
PrintResolutionCalculator.verdictSufficient: ✓ Your photo's resolution is enough for this print size.
PrintResolutionCalculator.verdictInsufficient: ⚠ Your photo's resolution falls short — see the upscaling guide below.
PrintResolutionCalculator.upscaleSufficient: No upscaling needed — your current resolution is already enough.
PrintResolutionCalculator.upscaleMinor: Just a small enlargement is needed — ordinary resizing should print cleanly at this level.
PrintResolutionCalculator.upscaleModerate: Some upscaling is needed — an AI upscaler (like Topaz Gigapixel) can give good results in this range.
PrintResolutionCalculator.upscaleMajor: The shortfall is significant — even upscaling may show visible quality loss. Consider printing at a smaller size, or re-shooting at a higher resolution if possible.
PrintResolutionCalculator.pageDescription: Enter your photo's pixel size and print DPI to find the maximum print size, or check whether your resolution is enough for a target print size.
PrintResolutionCalculator.aboutBody: Print sharpness depends on dots per inch (DPI): the same photo prints smaller at a higher DPI and larger at a lower one. This calculator uses your photo's pixel dimensions to find the maximum size you can print at a chosen DPI — and, the other way around, lets you pick a target print size (a photo-lab size or a standard paper size like A4) to see the minimum pixel size it needs and whether your current photo measures up.
PrintResolutionCalculator.disclaimer: 300 DPI is commonly treated as the 'photo quality' benchmark, but large prints viewed from a distance (posters, banners) often look just as sharp at 150–200 DPI. Actual print quality also depends on the print shop's equipment and paper.

faq.question: Do I really need 300 DPI?
faq.answer: Not always. 300 DPI is a common benchmark for prints viewed up close (albums, framed photos), but large posters or banners viewed from a distance can look plenty sharp at around 150 DPI. The farther the viewing distance, the lower the DPI you need.

faq.question: If my resolution is too low, do I always need to re-shoot?
faq.answer: No. If the shortfall is small (an upscale factor of 1.3x or less in the advanced section), ordinary resizing is often enough, and an AI upscaler is a solid option beyond that. Re-shooting or choosing a smaller print size is really only worth recommending once the factor passes about 2x.

faq.question: What's the difference between photo print sizes and paper sizes like A4?
faq.answer: Photo print sizes (4×6, 8×10, etc.) are the inch-based sizes common at photo labs, while sizes like A4/A3 are ISO standard sizes used for office and general printing. This calculator offers both as presets, plus a 'Custom' option for anything else.

PrintResolutionCalculator.exampleLeftAlt: A printed photo being examined closely for sharpness
PrintResolutionCalculator.exampleRightAlt: A large-format printer producing a photo print

sections.heading: How the calculation works
body: The maximum print size in inches is your photo's pixel count divided by DPI. Width and height are calculated separately, and a cm value is shown using 2.54 cm per inch. If you already have a target print size, width and height in inches × DPI gives the pixels you need, and the product of the two is the required megapixels.

The upscale factor in the advanced section is the square root of required megapixels divided by current megapixels. At 1 or below no enlargement is needed, up to 1.3 is minor, up to 2 is moderate, and above 2 is a major shortfall.

sections.heading: Worked examples
list: A 6000×4000 px photo (about 24 MP) can print up to about 20.0×13.3 in (about 50.8×33.9 cm) at 300 DPI, or about 40.0×26.7 in at 150 DPI.
An 8×10 in print at 300 DPI needs 2,400×3,000 px (7.2 MP), and A4 (8.27×11.69 in) needs about 2,480×3,508 px (8.7 MP). A 24 MP photo has plenty of headroom.
16×20 in needs 4,800×6,000 px (28.8 MP), an upscale factor of about 1.10 for a 24 MP photo, and A2 needs about 4,961×7,016 px (34.8 MP), about 1.20. Both are minor, so ordinary resizing is enough.
20×30 in needs 6,000×9,000 px (54 MP), about 1.5, and A1 needs about 7,016×9,933 px (69.7 MP), about 1.7. In this range an AI upscaler can help.

sections.heading: When to use it
body: Use it before ordering a framed print, an album or a poster, to check that your photo's resolution is enough. It is also handy when you wonder how large you can print, or when choosing a camera and estimating the megapixels a given print size needs.

sections.heading: Limits and common mistakes
list: 300 DPI is the benchmark for prints viewed up close. Large posters and banners viewed from a distance often look sharp at 150 to 200 DPI.
If you cropped the photo, enter the pixel size after cropping. Entering the original camera size will say you can print larger than you really can.
For print sizes with a different aspect ratio (for example a 3:2 photo printed at 4:5), the edges get cropped, so the actual layout can differ from the calculated result.
Falling short on pixels does not always mean re-shooting. At 1.3× or below, ordinary resizing is often enough.
Real print quality also depends on the print shop's equipment and paper.

StorageCalculator.invalidInput: Enter valid, positive numbers for every field.
StorageCalculator.backupCopiesHint: Calculated for {total} total copies, including the original.
StorageCalculator.pageDescription: Calculate the storage space and number of memory cards you'll need from your file format and shot count, plus backup copies and estimated cloud upload time.
StorageCalculator.aboutBody: Working out your storage needs before a shoot helps you avoid running out of memory cards or drive space partway through. This calculator uses your file format (JPEG, compressed RAW, or uncompressed RAW) and shot count to find the total storage needed and how many memory cards that takes. For multi-day trips or projects, you can enter an average daily shot count and number of days instead, and it'll work out the total shot count for you.
StorageCalculator.disclaimer: Actual file sizes vary by camera model, resolution, compression, and scene detail (busier scenes produce larger files in both RAW and JPEG). For a safety margin, consider planning for 10–20% more storage than the calculated figure.

faq.question: Should I calculate based on RAW or JPEG?
faq.answer: Use RAW if you plan to do significant editing afterward, or JPEG if you need ready-to-use results right away. If your camera saves both formats at once, add the two file sizes together and enter that total with the 'Custom' option.

faq.question: How many backup copies should I keep?
faq.answer: A common rule of thumb is at least 2–3 total copies including the original (for example: camera original + external drive + cloud). Entering 1 in the advanced 'Extra Backup Copies' field calculates storage for 2 total copies including the original.

faq.question: Why might the real upload time differ from the estimate?
faq.answer: This calculator assumes your entered upload speed holds steady the whole time, which is a theoretical estimate. Real-world uploads often take longer due to network congestion, Wi-Fi conditions, or the cloud service's own processing speed.

StorageCalculator.exampleLeftAlt: Several camera memory cards laid out together
StorageCalculator.exampleRightAlt: Photos being backed up to an external hard drive

sections.heading: How the calculation works
body: The math is simple. Original storage in GB is file size per shot (MB) × number of shots ÷ 1,000, and total storage is the original × (1 + extra backup copies). Cards needed is total storage divided by card size, rounded up. Using 1 GB = 1,000 MB matches how card makers label capacity.

The default file sizes assume a typical 24–45 MP full-frame or APS-C camera: about 8 MB for JPEG, 30 MB for compressed RAW and 65 MB for uncompressed RAW. Real sizes depend on your sensor and the scene, so use "Custom" if you know your actual file size.

sections.heading: Worked examples
list: Shooting 300 frames a day for 5 days is 1,500 shots. In compressed RAW (30 MB) the original is 45 GB; with one extra backup copy you need 90 GB, which one 128 GB card covers.
The same 1,500 shots as JPEG (8 MB) come to 12 GB, or 24 GB with a backup. Changing format alone cuts the storage to roughly a quarter.
In uncompressed RAW (65 MB) the original is 97.5 GB and 195 GB with a backup, which takes two 128 GB cards.
Uploading 90 GB (backup included) at 100 Mbps takes about 2 hours in theory (7,200 s). For 195 GB it is about 4 hours 20 minutes.

sections.heading: When to use it
body: Use it before a trip to decide how many cards to pack, to pick an external SSD size, or to estimate space before a shoot that produces hundreds of frames at once, like a timelapse. The daily-shots mode suits trips and projects where you shoot a similar amount every day.

sections.heading: Limits and common mistakes
list: If your camera saves RAW and JPEG together, add both file sizes and enter the total under "Custom". Calculating only one format can leave you short.
Usable space is a little below a card's labeled capacity, and filling a card to the brim is risky. As the page notes, plan for 10–20% more than the calculated figure.
Backup copies means extra copies beyond the original. Entering 1 calculates for 2 total copies including the original.
Upload time is a theoretical value that assumes your entered speed holds steady. Real uploads can take longer depending on the network.
Video is not included. If you also record video, add its storage separately.

ExifRemover.privacyNote: This tool never uploads your photos to a server — everything happens in your browser. Your files never leave your device.
ExifRemover.formatNote: Supported formats: JPEG, PNG, WebP. HEIC (iPhone's default format) and TIFF aren't supported yet.
ExifRemover.gpsOnlyLabel: Remove GPS location only (keep the rest of EXIF)
ExifRemover.gpsOnlyHint: JPEG only. Some files also mirror GPS coordinates into XMP — for guaranteed complete location removal, turn this off and use full removal instead.
ExifRemover.removeIptcLabel: Also remove IPTC/Photoshop metadata (copyright, captions, keywords, etc.)
ExifRemover.removeIptcHint: On by default. Turn this off if you want to keep copyright info attached to the photo.
ExifRemover.pageDescription: Safely strip EXIF, GPS location, and IPTC metadata from your photos right in your browser. Process multiple files at once and download them as a ZIP.
ExifRemover.aboutBody: Photos often carry hidden EXIF metadata — camera model, shooting settings, the date and time taken, and sometimes even the exact GPS location where the photo was captured. Stripping this before sharing a photo online prevents unwanted personal information from leaking out. This tool removes only the metadata sections at the byte level without re-compressing the image's pixel data, so there's zero quality loss. Everything runs in your browser — your photos are never sent to a server.
ExifRemover.disclaimer: HEIC (iPhone's default photo format) and TIFF aren't reliably supported by standard browser APIs yet, so they're not included. Convert those to JPEG first (from your phone or camera's settings) if you need to use this tool on them.

faq.question: Are my photos really never uploaded anywhere?
faq.answer: Correct. Everything runs as JavaScript inside your own browser — it reads and rebuilds the file locally with no network request involved. You can verify this yourself in your browser's developer tools Network tab.

faq.question: Does removing metadata reduce photo quality?
faq.answer: No. This tool doesn't re-compress the image at all — it only cuts out the byte ranges where metadata is stored, leaving the original pixel data completely untouched.

faq.question: I want to remove just the GPS data but keep the camera info.
faq.answer: Turn on the 'Remove GPS location only' checkbox in Advanced Options — for JPEG files, this strips just the GPS coordinates while leaving camera model, lens, and shooting settings intact.

ExifRemover.exampleLeftAlt: A photo's metadata panel showing camera settings and GPS location
ExifRemover.exampleRightAlt: A clean photo file with all metadata stripped out

sections.heading: What gets removed and how
body: The tool does not re-compress your image. It cuts out only the parts of the file that hold metadata, at the byte level, and copies the pixel data through unchanged, so quality does not change at all.

In JPEG it removes the APP1 segment (EXIF and XMP), the APP13 segment (IPTC) and text comments (COM), while leaving the JFIF header and the ICC color profile so colors stay the same. In PNG it removes text chunks (tEXt, zTXt, iTXt), the EXIF chunk and the modification-time chunk (tIME). In WebP it removes the EXIF and XMP chunks.

sections.heading: How to use it and the options
list: Supported formats are JPEG, PNG and WebP. You can add several files at once, process them, and download them one by one or as a ZIP.

"Remove GPS location only" deletes just the GPS coordinates in JPEG and keeps camera model, lens and shooting settings. Some editing tools also copy GPS into XMP, so for guaranteed location removal turn this off and use full removal.
"Remove IPTC" is on by default. Turn it off if you want copyright information to stay attached to the photo.
Before processing, the tool shows whether each photo has camera info or GPS, so you can see what will be removed.

sections.heading: When to use it
body: Use it before posting to social media, a blog or a marketplace to keep the location of photos taken near your home from leaking out. It is also useful before submitting photos to a stock site or a client when you want to tidy up equipment and settings information.

sections.heading: Limits and common mistakes
list: HEIC and TIFF are not supported. Convert iPhone HEIC photos to JPEG first.
The tool does not remove what is visible in the picture, such as faces, signs or license plates. It removes metadata only.
Some social networks strip metadata on upload, but this varies by service, so removing it yourself first is safer.
Your original stays untouched and you download a new file. Check the result before deleting the original.
Everything happens in your browser and your photos are never sent to a server.

CropFactorCalculator.equivalentApertureNote: On {sensor}, this looks roughly like {aperture} for depth of field / background blur.
CropFactorCalculator.pageDescription: Convert a focal length between full-frame, APS-C, and Micro Four Thirds equivalents.
CropFactorCalculator.aboutBody: The same lens shows a different field of view depending on your camera's sensor size. This tool calculates the 35mm (full-frame) equivalent focal length and field of view based on your sensor's crop factor, and also shows the focal length that would produce the same field of view on a different sensor system. The advanced options add the actual depth of field (hyperfocal distance, near/far limits) plus a reference aperture that would look similarly deep on another sensor.
CropFactorCalculator.disclaimer: Results are approximations based on standard formulas and may differ somewhat from real-world lens distortion or manufacturer-published specifications.

faq.question: How is the crop factor calculated?
faq.answer: It's the ratio between the sensor's diagonal length and a full-frame (36×24mm) sensor's diagonal (about 43.3mm). This closely matches the crop factors manufacturers officially quote (e.g. 1.5x for APS-C, 2.0x for Micro Four Thirds).

faq.question: What does the 'precise depth-of-field diagnosis' advanced option show?
faq.answer: It calculates the actual hyperfocal distance, near/far limits, and total depth of field for the sensor, focal length, aperture, and subject distance you entered. The circle-of-confusion value used is a standard approximation based on the sensor diagonal, so real-world results can vary with print size and viewing distance.

faq.question: Why is the 'equivalent aperture' different when compared to another sensor?
faq.answer: Depth of field and background blur are governed by the lens's actual physical aperture diameter, not the f-number alone. When the field of view is matched across different sensor sizes, the f-number that produces the same apparent depth of field scales with the ratio of the two sensors' crop factors.

CropFactorCalculator.exampleLeftAlt: The same lens framed on a full-frame camera
CropFactorCalculator.exampleRightAlt: The same lens framed on a crop-sensor camera, showing a narrower field of view

sections.heading: How the calculation works
body: Crop factor is the diagonal of a full-frame (36×24 mm) sensor, about 43.3 mm, divided by the diagonal of your sensor. The equivalent focal length is the real focal length times the crop factor, and field of view is 2 × atan(sensor dimension ÷ (2 × focal length)), calculated separately for width and height.

In the advanced options, the comparison sensor tells you which focal length gives the same field of view: your equivalent focal length divided by the comparison sensor's crop factor. The equivalent aperture multiplies your f-number by (your crop factor ÷ comparison crop factor) to show the f-number that gives similar depth of field for the same framing.

sections.heading: Worked examples
list: The crop factors for the sensor presets are full frame 1.00, Canon APS-C about 1.61, Nikon/Sony/Fuji APS-C about 1.53, Micro Four Thirds about 2.00, 1-inch about 2.73 and medium format about 0.79. These line up with the 1.5×, 1.6× and 2× figures manufacturers usually quote.
A 50 mm lens on a Nikon or Sony APS-C camera has an equivalent focal length of about 77 mm, with a field of view of about 26.4° wide and 17.7° tall. The same 50 mm on full frame is about 39.6° wide.
A 25 mm lens on Micro Four Thirds is equivalent to about 50 mm. To get that field of view on APS-C (Nikon/Sony) you would need a lens of about 33 mm.
Comparing a Micro Four Thirds 25 mm f/1.8 with full frame gives an equivalent aperture of about f/3.6, meaning background blur similar to f/3.6 on full frame for the same framing.

sections.heading: When to use it
body: Use it when switching to a camera with a different sensor size or buying a lens, to see what focal length gives your current field of view on another system. It also helps when you want to check the equivalent focal lengths quoted in photo descriptions for different sensors.

sections.heading: Limits and common mistakes
list: Crop factor applies to field of view only. It does not change the lens's real focal length or exposure (f-number, shutter speed, ISO), so your exposure settings stay the same.
Equivalent aperture is for comparing depth of field and background blur, not for exposure. The same f/1.8 on a smaller sensor gives deeper depth of field.
Do not mix up the focal length printed on the lens with the equivalent focal length. Depth-of-field and astro calculators need the real focal length.
Canon APS-C and other makers' APS-C sensors differ slightly in size, so their crop factors are 1.61 and 1.53.
Results are approximations from standard formulas and can differ a little from real lens distortion or manufacturer-published specifications.

DofHyperfocalTable.pageTitle: Depth of Field & Hyperfocal Distance Tables
DofHyperfocalTable.pageDescription: See hyperfocal distance across every standard aperture, and near/far focus limits across a range of subject distances, in one table — for your focal length and sensor size.
DofHyperfocalTable.aboutBody: This page shows the same hyperfocal-distance and depth-of-field formulas used by our single-value DoF calculator, laid out as tables so you can compare every standard aperture or subject distance at a glance instead of entering one value at a time. The hyperfocal table only depends on focal length, aperture, and sensor size; the depth-of-field table also uses the aperture you select above.
DofHyperfocalTable.disclaimer: For reference only. Real-world sharpness can vary with your specific lens and how the final image is viewed or printed.

faq.question: How is this different from the single-value DoF calculator?
faq.answer: It uses the exact same formulas, but shows every standard aperture's hyperfocal distance, and every preset subject distance's near/far limits, in table form instead of one result at a time.

faq.question: Why doesn't the hyperfocal table need a subject distance?
faq.answer: Hyperfocal distance depends only on focal length, aperture, and sensor size (via the circle of confusion) — not on how far away your subject is.

faq.question: Can I use a custom sensor size?
faq.answer: Yes — choose "Custom" under Sensor Size and enter your own circle of confusion value in millimeters.

DofHyperfocalTable.exampleLeftAlt: Landscape photo focused at the hyperfocal distance, sharp from the foreground to infinity
DofHyperfocalTable.exampleRightAlt: Landscape photo focused too close, leaving the distant background out of focus

sections.heading: How to read the hyperfocal table
body: The hyperfocal distance is the focus distance that keeps everything out to infinity acceptably sharp while stretching the in-focus zone as close to you as possible. Focus there and the zone from half that distance to infinity falls within acceptable sharpness. Each row of the table gives this distance in meters for one aperture.

The formula is H = f² / (N × c), plus f. Here f is focal length, N is the f-number and c is the circle of confusion in millimeters. A longer focal length or a wider aperture pushes the hyperfocal distance farther away, and stopping down brings it closer.

sections.heading: Worked examples
list: Full frame, 24mm at f/8: the hyperfocal distance is about 2.42 m. Focus at 2.42 m and everything from roughly 1.2 m to infinity is acceptably sharp.

Sensor size matters at 35mm and f/8: about 5.14 m on full frame, but about 7.69 m on APS-C (using a 0.02 mm circle of confusion). A smaller sensor allows a smaller circle of confusion, which pushes the hyperfocal distance out.
Full frame, 50mm at f/2.8: about 29.81 m. Stop the same lens down to f/8 and it drops to about 10.47 m.

sections.heading: How to read the depth-of-field table
body: The depth-of-field table uses the aperture you chose above and lists the near limit, far limit and total depth of field at nine subject distances from 0.5 m to 100 m. When the subject distance is at or beyond the hyperfocal distance, the far limit reads "Infinity".

For example, a full-frame 50mm lens focused on a subject 5 m away keeps about 3.39 m to 9.49 m sharp at f/8 (about 6.10 m in total), but only about 4.29 m to 6.00 m at f/2.8 (about 1.71 m in total). One aperture change at the same distance changes the sharp zone dramatically.

sections.heading: Limits and common mistakes
list: The circle of confusion values are common approximations for each sensor size. If you plan to print large or inspect images at 100%, choose "Custom" and enter a smaller value to be more conservative.
When you focus at the hyperfocal distance, the near limit sits at about half that distance. If a very close foreground matters, check that point before you shoot.
Stopping down too far lets diffraction soften the whole image. The smallest aperture in the table is not always the best choice.
These are theoretical reference values. Lens behavior and real focusing accuracy vary, so check important frames by zooming in after you shoot.

Sunny16Calculator.baselineNote: Based on the {aperture} baseline for this lighting condition at ISO 100, adjusted for your chosen ISO and aperture.
Sunny16Calculator.invalidInput: Choose a valid lighting condition, ISO, and aperture.
Sunny16Calculator.pageDescription: Estimate a correct exposure without a light meter, using the classic Sunny 16 rule and its overcast/shade variants — just pick your lighting condition, ISO, and aperture.
Sunny16Calculator.aboutBody: The Sunny 16 rule is a decades-old rule of thumb: on a bright sunny day, setting your aperture to f/16 and your shutter speed to roughly 1/ISO gives a correctly exposed photo. Its lesser-known variants extend the same idea to overcast and shaded conditions at wider apertures (f/11, f/8, f/5.6, f/4). This calculator applies the same stop-for-stop math our exposure triangle calculator uses to adjust the baseline for whatever ISO and aperture you actually want to shoot at.
Sunny16Calculator.disclaimer: An estimate for typical outdoor daylight conditions — always check your camera's meter or a test shot when it matters.

faq.question: Does the Sunny 16 rule still matter with modern light meters?
faq.answer: It's mainly useful as a sanity check, for manual-exposure film cameras without a working meter, or when you want a fast starting point before fine-tuning.

faq.question: Why do the overcast variants use different apertures?
faq.answer: Each stop of the aperture roughly corresponds to a lighting condition letting in about half as much light as the one before it, so the rule widens the aperture by one stop per condition to keep the same shutter speed reasonable.

faq.question: What if I want a specific shutter speed instead of a specific aperture?
faq.answer: Pick the aperture that gives you a shutter speed close to what you want — since the underlying math is stop-for-stop, you can also work backward from a target shutter speed using our exposure triangle calculator.

Sunny16Calculator.exampleLeftAlt: Photo taken outdoors in bright, direct sunlight
Sunny16Calculator.exampleRightAlt: Photo taken outdoors under overcast, cloudy skies

sections.heading: How the calculation works
body: For each lighting condition the calculator starts from a baseline aperture (sunny f/16, slight overcast f/11, overcast f/8, heavy overcast f/5.6, open shade or sunset f/4) with a shutter speed of about 1/100 s at ISO 100. It then recalculates the shutter speed, stop for stop, for the aperture and ISO you choose.
Opening the aperture by one stop halves the shutter time, and so does raising ISO by one stop. The calculator applies both in turn to reach the final value.

sections.heading: Worked examples
list: In sunny conditions (f/16) at ISO 100 and f/16, the shutter speed is about 1/100 s. This is the classic Sunny 16 rule.
In sunny conditions at ISO 400 and f/8, it is about 1/1600 s. Opening two stops and raising ISO two stops makes the shutter four stops faster.
In sunny conditions at ISO 100, opening to f/5.6 gives about 1/800 s. It shows how fast the shutter has to be when you open up for a blurrier background.
On an overcast day (f/8) at ISO 400 and f/2.8, the result is about 1/3200 s.
In open shade (f/4) at ISO 100 and f/4, it is about 1/100 s, and at ISO 800 with f/2 it is about 1/3200 s.

sections.heading: When to use it
body: Use it as a quick reference with film cameras that have no meter, when shooting in manual exposure, or when your camera's auto exposure looks off. It is also good practice to memorize rough starting values for each lighting condition before heading outdoors.

sections.heading: Limits and common mistakes
list: The values are estimates for typical outdoor daytime light. They may not hold for low sun in the morning or evening, strong reflections from snow or sand, or backlit scenes.
If your subject is unusually dark or bright, check with your camera's meter or a test shot and apply exposure compensation if needed.
Choosing the wrong lighting condition shifts the result by a stop or two. Judging by how sharp the edges of shadows are can help.
If the shutter speed comes out too slow, camera shake can appear. Raise ISO or open the aperture.
The displayed shutter speed is rounded to a near standard step. On a real camera, pick the closest available value.

AdvancedDofDiffractionCalculator.diffractionWarning: At {aperture}, diffraction has started to soften fine detail for this sensor size. This becomes more visible the further past the diffraction-limited aperture you go.
AdvancedDofDiffractionCalculator.diffractionOk: At {aperture}, you're within this sensor's diffraction limit — diffraction isn't yet the main factor softening detail.
AdvancedDofDiffractionCalculator.pageDescription: Find your sensor's diffraction-limited aperture and see the resulting depth of field together — the same circle-of-confusion math behind our standard DoF calculator, extended with diffraction.
AdvancedDofDiffractionCalculator.aboutBody: Every lens is sharpest wide open in terms of diffraction, and gets softer past a certain aperture as the diffraction pattern (the "Airy disk") grows larger than the circle of confusion your sensor size can resolve. This calculator finds that diffraction-limited aperture for your sensor, using the standard Rayleigh-criterion approximation (Airy disk diameter ≈ 2.44 × wavelength × f-number, with a 550nm reference wavelength), and shows the classic hyperfocal-based depth of field for your chosen aperture and subject distance side by side — so you can weigh "more depth of field" against "more diffraction softening" for the same shot.
AdvancedDofDiffractionCalculator.disclaimer: An approximation using a fixed reference wavelength and standard circle-of-confusion values — real-world sharpness also depends on your specific lens, sensor resolution, and how the image is viewed or printed.

faq.question: What does "diffraction-limited aperture" mean?
faq.answer: It's the narrowest aperture (smallest f-number) past which diffraction becomes the main thing softening fine detail in a photo, for a given sensor size. Stopping down further still deepens depth of field, but at the cost of increasingly visible softening.

faq.question: Why is the diffraction-limited aperture different for each sensor size?
faq.answer: It depends on the circle of confusion, which is based on sensor size (via the same values our DoF calculator uses) — a smaller sensor has a smaller circle of confusion, so diffraction becomes visible at a wider aperture (a lower f-number) than on a larger sensor.

faq.question: Should I avoid diffraction-limited apertures entirely?
faq.answer: Not necessarily — depth of field is often more important to the final image than the small amount of softening near the diffraction limit. It matters most when you need maximum resolved detail, such as large prints or heavy crops.

AdvancedDofDiffractionCalculator.exampleLeftAlt: Photo shot at a wide aperture with sharp detail and shallow depth of field
AdvancedDofDiffractionCalculator.exampleRightAlt: Photo shot at a very narrow aperture, softened by diffraction across the whole frame

sections.heading: How the calculation works
body: The Airy disk diameter is about 2.44 × wavelength × f-number, using a reference wavelength of 550 nm, the middle of visible light. The f-number at which that diameter equals the circle of confusion set by your sensor size is the diffraction-limited aperture: circle of confusion ÷ (2.44 × wavelength).

Depth of field uses the same hyperfocal formulas as the DoF calculator, so the diffraction limit and depth of field appear side by side for the same aperture. You can weigh the sharpness you lose to diffraction against the depth of field you gain by stopping down.

sections.heading: Worked examples
list: The diffraction-limited apertures by sensor are about f/22.4 for full frame, f/26.8 for medium format, f/14.9 for APS-C, f/11.2 for Micro Four Thirds and f/8.2 for 1-inch. The smaller the sensor, the sooner diffraction shows.

At f/16 the Airy disk is about 0.0215 mm (21.5 μm). That is smaller than the full-frame circle of confusion of 0.03 mm, so it is within the limit, but on APS-C (0.02 mm) it is about 7% past the limit and on Micro Four Thirds (0.015 mm) about 43% past.
On full frame with a 24 mm lens focused at 3 m, the near limit is about 1.35 m at f/8, about 0.87 m at f/16 and about 0.69 m at f/22. Beyond f/8, each extra stop buys less and less depth of field.
On APS-C with a 35 mm lens focused at 2 m, the sharp zone at f/8 is about 1.59 to 2.69 m, widening to about 1.33 to 4.07 m at f/16. But f/16 is past this sensor's diffraction limit of about f/14.9.

sections.heading: When to use it
body: It is most useful in landscape and architecture work when deciding how far you can stop down for depth of field. If you plan large prints or heavy crops, you can check in advance how much an aperture past the diffraction limit will cost you.

sections.heading: Limits and common mistakes
list: Passing the diffraction limit does not make a photo unusable. Softness grows gradually, and when depth of field matters more, an aperture past the limit can be the better choice.
The calculation is an approximation using a fixed wavelength and a standard circle of confusion, so real lens resolution and sensor megapixels will change the outcome.
A lens's sharpest aperture is usually two or three stops down from wide open, which is a separate factor from the diffraction limit.
Results assume screen-size viewing. At 100% zoom, diffraction can show at an earlier aperture.
A custom circle of confusion must be between 0.001 and 0.1 mm. Use it only when you know the right value for your sensor.

CameraFovCalculator.tableSubtitle: Horizontal, vertical, and diagonal field of view at common focal lengths, for your selected sensor size.
CameraFovCalculator.pageDescription: See the horizontal, vertical, and diagonal angle of view your lens captures on your sensor — in degrees, at any focal length.
CameraFovCalculator.aboutBody: Field of view (FOV) is the angle of the scene your lens actually captures, measured in degrees, and it depends on both the focal length and your sensor's physical size. This calculator uses the standard trigonometric formula (FOV = 2 x arctan(sensor dimension / (2 x focal length))) applied separately to your sensor's width, height, and diagonal. It's the same math behind our crop-factor calculator's field-of-view figures, on its own page for anyone who wants the angle of view directly — useful for planning shots where you need to know how wide a lens will frame a scene (surveying, videography, architectural photography) without needing the crop-factor/equivalent-focal-length context as well.
CameraFovCalculator.disclaimer: Calculated from the sensor's physical dimensions and focal length only — it doesn't account for lens distortion or the small field-of-view reduction some lenses show at their closest focus distance.

faq.question: What's the difference between this and the crop-factor calculator?
faq.answer: They use the same underlying formula, but this page is built around the field-of-view angle itself (useful when you need to know exactly how wide a shot will be), while the crop-factor calculator is built around comparing equivalent focal lengths and apertures across sensor sizes.

faq.question: Why are there three FOV values — horizontal, vertical, and diagonal?
faq.answer: Horizontal and vertical FOV describe how wide and how tall the frame is, using the sensor's width and height respectively. Diagonal FOV (using the sensor's diagonal measurement) is the single number most commonly quoted for a lens's overall angle of view, since it doesn't depend on whether the camera is held horizontally or vertically.

faq.question: Can I use this for a specific camera model instead of a general sensor size?
faq.answer: Yes — select "Custom" under Sensor Size and enter your camera's exact sensor width and height in millimeters, which you can usually find in its manufacturer specifications.

CameraFovCalculator.exampleLeftAlt: Photo taken with a wide-angle lens showing a broad field of view
CameraFovCalculator.exampleRightAlt: Photo taken with a telephoto lens showing a narrow, zoomed-in field of view

sections.heading: How the calculation works
body: Field of view is 2 × atan(sensor dimension ÷ (2 × focal length)). The same formula is applied to the sensor's width, height and diagonal to give horizontal, vertical and diagonal field of view.

Field of view depends on both focal length and sensor size: longer focal lengths narrow it, and larger sensors widen it. The table below the calculator shows the field of view at common focal lengths from 14 mm to 300 mm for the sensor you pick.

sections.heading: Worked examples
list: On full frame, 24 mm gives about 73.7° horizontal, 53.1° vertical and 84.1° diagonal. 50 mm gives about 39.6° horizontal, 27.0° vertical and 46.8° diagonal.
On full frame, 85 mm is about 28.6° diagonal, 200 mm about 12.3° and 14 mm about 114.2°. Diagonal is the figure most often quoted in lens descriptions.
On APS-C (23.5×15.6 mm), 50 mm gives about 26.4° horizontal, 17.7° vertical and 31.5° diagonal, framing narrower than the same lens on full frame.
A 25 mm lens on Micro Four Thirds (17.3×13 mm) gives about 46.8° diagonal, the same as 50 mm on full frame.

sections.heading: When to use it
body: It is useful for architecture and interior work, video and site documentation, anywhere you need to know how wide a scene will be framed as an angle. If you need the angle itself rather than crop factor or equivalent focal length, you can read it directly.

sections.heading: Limits and common mistakes
list: Do not mix up vertical and horizontal field of view. Turning the camera vertical swaps the two, but the diagonal stays the same.
The field of view quoted in lens marketing is usually diagonal. Comparing against a horizontal figure makes the numbers look different.
The calculation uses only sensor size and focal length. It does not account for lens distortion or the slight narrowing some lenses show at close focus.
For a specific camera, choose "Custom" under sensor size and enter the manufacturer's sensor width and height in millimeters.
The focal length to enter is the real one. Entering an equivalent focal length makes the field of view look too narrow for the sensor.

FlashGuideNumberCalculator.guideNumberHint: Check your flash's manual or spec sheet for its published guide number — most list it at ISO 100 for a specific zoom head setting (commonly 35mm or 50mm).
FlashGuideNumberCalculator.invalidInput: Enter a valid guide number and ISO.
FlashGuideNumberCalculator.pageDescription: Work out how far your flash can properly light a subject at a given aperture, or which aperture to use at a given distance — using your flash's published guide number.
FlashGuideNumberCalculator.aboutBody: A flash's guide number (GN) is the classic way manufacturers rate manual flash output: Guide Number = f-stop x distance, at a stated reference ISO (almost always ISO 100) and, for zoom-head flashes, a stated zoom setting. Rearranging that formula lets you solve for whichever value you need — the farthest distance a given aperture will properly expose, or the aperture required at a given distance. Guide numbers also scale with sensitivity as the square root of the ISO ratio, so this calculator adjusts your flash's rated guide number to whatever ISO you're actually shooting at before doing the distance/aperture math. Pair this with our exposure triangle calculator if you also need to work out how ambient light and flash exposure interact.
FlashGuideNumberCalculator.disclaimer: Guide numbers are manufacturer-published ratings measured under controlled conditions — real-world results vary with room reflectivity, subject size, flash zoom setting, and diffusers or modifiers.

faq.question: Where do I find my flash's guide number?
faq.answer: It's in the flash's manual or manufacturer spec sheet, usually listed at ISO 100 for a specific zoom head position (often 35mm or 50mm equivalent). If your flash has a zoom head, the guide number changes at each zoom setting — use the value for whatever zoom position you're actually shooting at.

faq.question: Why does the guide number change with ISO?
faq.answer: A higher ISO makes the sensor more sensitive to the same amount of light, which is equivalent to boosting the flash's effective reach — but only by the square root of the ISO ratio, not proportionally. Doubling ISO increases the usable guide number (and distance) by about 41%, not 100%.

faq.question: Does this account for bounce flash or light modifiers?
faq.answer: No — guide numbers assume direct, undiffused flash in open conditions. Bouncing the flash off a ceiling or wall, or adding a diffuser/softbox, reduces the effective light reaching your subject, so you'll typically need a wider aperture or closer distance than this calculator suggests.

FlashGuideNumberCalculator.exampleLeftAlt: Photo taken close to the flash, evenly and brightly lit
FlashGuideNumberCalculator.exampleRightAlt: Photo taken far from the flash, appearing dim and underexposed

sections.heading: How the calculation works
body: Guide number (GN) equals f-number × distance. Knowing GN, distance = GN ÷ f-number and f-number = GN ÷ distance. Manufacturers usually publish GN at ISO 100, so when you change ISO the calculator uses GN × √(ISO ÷ 100).
GN and distance are handled in the same unit, either meters or feet. One meter is about 3.28 feet.

sections.heading: Worked examples
list: A flash with GN 58 (m, ISO 100) used at f/8 can properly light a subject up to about 7.25 m away.
Raising the same flash to ISO 400 doubles GN to about 116, so at f/8 it reaches about 14.5 m. Four times the ISO but only twice the GN is the square-root relationship.
With a GN 60 (m, ISO 100) flash and a subject 5 m away, the aperture needed is f/12. At ISO 400 you need f/24.
Going from ISO 100 to 200 multiplies GN by about 1.41, so GN 58 becomes about 82.
A flash rated GN 190 (feet, ISO 100) used at f/5.6 reaches about 33.9 ft.

sections.heading: When to use it
body: It helps when using flash in manual mode or with an off-camera strobe, to judge at which aperture and distance you get enough light. It is also good for building a reference chart ahead of time for events where distances change often.

sections.heading: Limits and common mistakes
list: A zoom-head flash has a different GN at each zoom position. Enter the GN for the zoom position you are actually using.
Published GN is measured under ideal conditions. Room reflectivity, subject size and diffusers can make real results differ a lot.
Bouncing off a ceiling or wall, or using a diffuser or softbox, reduces the light reaching your subject. You may need a wider aperture or a closer distance than the result suggests.
Lowering flash power lowers GN. If you entered the full-power GN, assume a shorter distance at fractional power (1/2, 1/4 and so on).
Shutter speed does not affect this calculation, but going above your flash sync speed can block part of the frame.

ShutterCountChecker.pageDescription: Find out how many shutter actuations your camera has recorded, directly from a NEF, CR3, or JPEG file — entirely in your browser. Currently supports Nikon and select Canon EOS R bodies, with more brands on the way.
ShutterCountChecker.aboutBody: Every camera's shutter (or, on many mirrorless bodies, the sensor's exposure count) is rated for a certain number of actuations before it's likely to need servicing. Manufacturers embed this running total in the file's metadata on many models, hidden inside a manufacturer-specific block that ordinary EXIF viewers don't parse. This tool reads that value directly out of the file's raw bytes: for Nikon cameras, from a documented, unencrypted field in the MakerNote; for Canon EOS R5, R6, R6 Mark II, R8, and R50 (CR3 files), from a publicly documented location inside the camera's CR3 container. This lets you check a used camera's shutter count yourself before buying it, or keep an eye on your own body's wear over time. It never sends your photo anywhere; everything happens in your browser.
ShutterCountChecker.disclaimer: Shutter count support depends on the camera manufacturer and model. Some older or lower-end bodies never record this value at all, regardless of which tool you use. Canon EOS R5/R6 support is based on published camera data rather than verified against every individual unit and firmware version — if a count looks wrong, please let us know.

faq.question: Why does this only support Nikon and a few Canon models right now?
faq.answer: Nikon documents this field (ShutterCount) as a plain, unencrypted number inside its MakerNote block, which we've independently verified against real camera files. Canon publishes the storage location for a handful of recent EOS R bodies — the R5, R6, R6 Mark II, R8, and R50 — so we support those too. Other manufacturers (Sony, Fujifilm, Olympus, Panasonic, Pentax) either don't store an equivalent value in the file at all, or store it in a way that varies by model and needs separate work per camera — we're expanding brand support gradually.

faq.question: Does this support Canon cameras?
faq.answer: Yes, for a handful of models. Currently supported: the EOS R5, EOS R6, EOS R6 Mark II, EOS R8, and EOS R50 (CR3 files only). Unlike Nikon, Canon stores this value at a different byte location for nearly every camera model, and a publicly documented location currently exists only for those five bodies. Every other Canon camera, old or new, isn't mapped yet — we'll add more as documented locations become available.

faq.question: Does this work with JPEG files, or only RAW?
faq.answer: Both. In-camera JPEGs carry the same MakerNote data as NEF files, as long as they haven't been re-saved or edited by another program (which typically strips or rewrites this metadata).

faq.question: Is my photo uploaded anywhere?
faq.answer: No. The file is read and parsed entirely in your browser using JavaScript — it's never sent to any server, matching how every other tool on ExifLens handles your files.

body: Many cameras record the shutter count in a manufacturer-specific area inside the photo file, called the MakerNote. Ordinary EXIF viewers do not interpret that area, so the value stays hidden, but this tool reads the file's raw bytes and finds it directly.

For Nikon it reads the unencrypted shutter count field inside the MakerNote. For Canon it reads a publicly documented storage location in CR3 files from the EOS R5, R6, R6 Mark II, R8 and R50. Everything runs in your browser and your photo is never sent anywhere.

sections.heading: When to use it
body: It is useful before buying a used camera, to check the shutter count yourself from the original photo the seller sends. You can also use it to keep an eye on your own camera's usage over time.

sections.heading: Limits and common mistakes
list: Photos that went through editing or social media may have had their metadata removed, so the value can be missing. Use the original file straight from the camera.
Shutter count is only a reference for judging a camera's condition. Rated shutter durability differs by model, and passing it does not mean the camera fails right away.
Some mirrorless bodies count sensor exposures rather than mechanical shutter actuations, so the number can mean something different.
Some older or entry-level models never record this value at all, so no tool can read it.
Canon R5/R6 support is based on published data and has not been verified against every individual unit and firmware version. If a count looks wrong, let us know.

GoldenHourCalculator.aboutTitle: About golden hour and blue hour
GoldenHourCalculator.aboutBody: Golden hour is the period shortly after sunrise and before sunset when the sun sits low on the horizon, giving warm, soft light. Blue hour is the brief window just after sunset (or just before sunrise) when the sky takes on a deep blue tone. This calculator uses your date and location to compute the exact time ranges where the sun's altitude falls in each of these bands — in order: morning blue hour, morning golden hour, evening golden hour, evening blue hour. Your location is only used for this calculation in your browser; it's never sent to a server.
GoldenHourCalculator.disclaimer: These times are based purely on the sun's geometric position — the actual color and softness of the light you experience still depends on weather, atmospheric conditions, and local terrain. As noted above, displayed times follow this device's own time zone, so keep that in mind when checking a different region ahead of a trip.

faq.question: Exactly when are golden hour and blue hour?
faq.answer: Golden hour runs while the sun's altitude is between about -0.83° and +6° above the horizon; blue hour runs between about -6° and -0.83°. Both the length and timing of each window vary by date and location.

faq.question: Why do the times look wrong when I enter coordinates for another region?
faq.answer: This calculator is a lightweight design that doesn't use a time-zone database — it displays the computed times in this device's (browser's) own current time zone. That's accurate for your immediate surroundings when you use "Use my location," but if you manually enter coordinates for a completely different time zone, the times shown reflect this device's time zone rather than the local time at that location.

faq.question: Is my location sent to a server?
faq.answer: No. Your latitude and longitude are only used for the calculation in your browser — they're never sent or stored anywhere. The "Use my location" button simply uses your browser's standard location permission prompt.

faq.question: Do I have to grant location permission to use this?
faq.answer: No — you can enter latitude and longitude manually and use the calculator without granting location permission at all.
